utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if I may say something briefly. I already have a very short time for cross-examination. Through the previous witness, we heard that the French confirmed that these traces were chipped, that the place of inspect was tampered with by chipping. Why don't we have the date here? I can't cover everything in my cross-examination, and I think this is an appropriate moment for me to ask about the missing date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find your intervention this time sort of obstructive. It's for you to further cross-examine the witness. Let's continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could play that clip to the end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to play the third clip, which is from 8 minutes and 50 seconds to 9 minutes and 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what we were looking at in that portion of the video?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: What we are seeing right now, body parts and the head?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just the portion of that video until the image arrived on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: When the FrenchBat team arrived from UNPROFOR, a French soldier or an officer - I don't remember exactly - used an army knife in an attempt to extract the part of the shell that was stuck at the place of impact. And the crime scene officer, Sead Besic, was the one standing next to him. And you could also see that the stabiliser was found in the center of the crater, which means that the French soldier managed to mark it with his knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you carry out measurements as to how far the stabiliser had penetrated into the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was nine centimetres with relation to the surface on the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to request 65 ter 09620, which is a photograph. If we could go to page 12 of that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we switch to e-court from Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go on another page, please. Sorry, sorry, we can hold it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is that that is in front of you at this point, Mr. Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We see the shell stabiliser to the center of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you identify what that is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The stabiliser of a 120-millimetre mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if we could have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what that is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The same as in the previous photo, only viewed from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if we could go to the first page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This refers -- this is a file of photo documentation of the Markale incident of the 5th of February, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. And the photo documentation was compiled by crime-scene officer Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, we have about 20 minutes' time today, so why don't you start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let's pause between questions and answers so that we can make it possible for the interpreters to do their job. First of all, let me thank you for meeting with my associates. I hope that would facilitate this cross-examination. And I would also like to tell you, in advance, that I'm not disputing anything on a personal basis. I'm only disputing facts. Therefore, rest assured that my intention is not to display anything but respect for your person.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today, my learned friend Prosecutor Gaynor described you as a forensic and ballistic analyst. Let me tell you why I noticed that, specifically. And the reason is because, in these reports, you have been characterised or described only as a ballistic expert. Is there any difference?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, I'll correct this in order to make it simple. The exact name of the title of the job that I had was an expert for mechanical traces and ballistics. The ballistics section for analysing traces was part of the forensic laboratory of the CSB Sarajevo and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So does either of these two qualify you for providing independent forensic findings for the use in courts?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, because the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time issued certificates to us that we, as active-duty police officers, could prepare documents that could be used in court proceedings at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, don't you find it to be more appropriately done by a proper institution, not to be done by the minister?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, that is your conclusion, and that is what was done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you talked to representatives of the Defence team, you said that you served as an infantry signalman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, if you're referring to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During your regular military service, did you undergo any training in shooting? And tell me from which weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Only from infantry weapons, like M-72, submachine-gun, light machine-gun, automatic rifle; that is to say, the weapons that the signals platoon had within infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, you underwent a communications course?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's how the JNA operate. The rest of my military service I spent in training on communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long does this firing training last?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The total initial training started -- lasted 30 days, and the shooting training lasted for about 15 days. But I must say that later I received some broader training, but again in the domain of infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you remained as part of the reserve forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, until the break-up of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: A corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you regularly summoned to take part in exercises?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Between 1985, when I finished my service, and the break-out -- the outbreak of war, two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2, you said that approximately for 13 months, you were a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, I was a member of the BH Territorial Defence, and then from July 1992, when the Army of BH was formed, I became a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which unit did you serve?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That was Bratstvo-Jedinstvo Territorial Defence, named after our local commune, and after that it was the 1st Motorised Brigade, and I served as a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that your local commune, Bratstvo-Jedinstvo, had its own territorial defence unit even in peace time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly whether it had, but it probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this Territorial Defence unit have its own weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, only a few weapons were there, rifles, hunting rifles, and a few semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was the 1st Motorised Brigade deployed? Where was its zone of responsibility? And please wait for the interpretation to finish. I believe you can answer now.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The area of responsibility was the line on the Miljacka River, from the Vrbanja Bridge via Hrasno Brdo, that area. We were deployed on the line from the Economics School to the Elektroprivreda building, and then we were transferred to Hrasno Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So from Vrbanja Bridge down to Elektroprivreda and so on, between you and the Serbs, the Serb Army, that is, there was only the Miljacka River, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. Between us and the units of the army of Republika Srpska, there was only the Miljacka River on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in July 1993, you went to the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your first job at the MUP was the first job you had after you got your degree in mechanical engineering within the stream for production, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, that was my first job after I basically graduated in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The plan was for you to get a job in Unioninvest, but the war made that impossible; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, yes. That is what I told your colleagues when I met up with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Unioninvest building is near Vrbanja Bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, that was the Unioninvest building, but now it's the Office of the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose control was that building during the war? In whose territory was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That building was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about those red buildings in the neighbourhood; were they under the BH Army or the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I think that the BH Army held positions above the Energopetrol gasoline station, whereas this part of Kovacici was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see later on whether that was actually the case. However, tell us, while you were at university, was there a subject that trained people in ballistics professionally?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: There wasn't a subject by that name, exactly, but there was a stream that trained engineers that could later work in specific industries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you did not study that particular stream; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did a general course in mechanical engineering; production, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At university, you did not take any courses in defence technology; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That's right, I did not have that subject while I was at university.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like us to review what we heard today during the cross-examination -- or, rather, the examination-in-chief. Let us try to clarify a few matters. You said, on page 69 -- or, rather, do we agree that the war ended in Sarajevo sometime towards the end of October, by a cease-fire, and then on the 21st of November, by the Dayton Peace Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when Grbavica was re-integrated, as you put it, when we handed Grbavica over to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I think it was the end of February or beginning of March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here that in these skyscrapers, one of the four, you found something that would correspond to sniper nests; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now assist us with this so that we would be as specific as possible? On which floors were these apartments in which you discovered that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We toured all four buildings. Of course, we didn't see each and every apartment. All the nests that we found were above the 10th floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the openings that you described, which direction did they face?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: They faced the Street of Vojvoda Putnika or, rather, the Smaja od Bosne, the entire segment on the right bank of the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that was the northern wall of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: If you're looking from the direction of Grbavica, then it's the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, any direction.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were these buildings? They face the river, don't they? The broader side faced the south and the other one faced the north; right? The north and south are something that we cannot bargain about; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: All the openings faced the north when viewed from that apartment; that is to say, from the direction of Grbavica towards the other bank of the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there were different openings; a small one, a bigger one, and at a third level there was the biggest one of all, and there were sandbags. Can you tell us, what does that look like, the small opening and the medium-sized opening? How big are they, and how high up were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Later on, I realised that that was called a tunnel. I found that particular terminology, and I was actually asked about that during one of my testimonies. The Defence asked me whether I had heard of that expression. The smallest opening was on the wall that is the external wall of the building, facing towards the north, towards the river, that is, and it was 20 by 20, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry. How high up was it in relation to the floor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I think between 80 and 100 centimetres, as far as I can remember; from the floor of that particular apartment, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, in the room next-door, there was an opening in the wall that was 40 by 40 or 50 by 50, roughly, again the external wall. And then if you look at the third room, because they operate from in depth, the opening is 80 by 80, and that's where the sandbags were and the parapets, if I can put it that way. So if you're looking at things from the point of view of the shooter, it looks like a tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far away were these sandbags from that opening?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: They were right by the opening, itself. There wasn't a particular distance. I cannot remember. I didn't even measure it or anything like that. However, I think that they were right by the wall and the opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there's an 80 centimetres, and then the next one?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The first one is 20 by 20, and the other one is 40 by 40, and then the third one is 80 by 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the floor, the first one is at 80 centimetres? I mean the distance from the floor.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, it goes down, doesn't it? If it was 1.1 metres, then you have to take away the 40 centimetres. And then over there you have the other 40 centimetres. So then the shooter has his rifle at a parallel level; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that dealt with -- I mean the crime scene, was it dealt with properly? Were photographs taken, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I'm sure, but I never saw this. I asked why not, but I never received any information in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that at Metalka, in an apartment, there were empty casings found from automatic weapons ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this photographed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, likewise, because, as I said, the entire team was there, headed by the investigating judge. There was also a crime scene officer and a member of the Security of Novo Sarajevo-Grbavica because that is the area that it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you -- do we have these photographs?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I have not seen them, just like the previous ones that I haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were these empty casings dealt with properly? We could have found some imprints there; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Of course they could have been found. I don't know about that particular information, that is to say, whether there was a finger-printing analysis that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that your army and ours did not have weaponry that could have been used as snipers with this kind of automatic ammunition? That kind of thing does exist in the world. However, in the Balkans, in the JNA, there was no such thing; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Ammunition of a 7.9-millimetre calibre is used by an M-76.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you said that the casings came from ammunition for automatic weapons, so what exists in that respect in our parts?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: An M-74 machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What calibre is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No one has any casing of all of those, not even as a souvenir?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't. Perhaps we can ask around in the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, are we done for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something before the adjournment, just a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The importance of this witness, both as an eye-witness and as a participant and as an investigator, is enormous. The distinguished Mr. Gaynor tried to deal with a great many facts with this witness, and my estimate of 20 hours is a conservative one, a modest one, therefore, if we also take into account the incidents that are not in my indictment. However, in order for the plot to thicken, I think that I would need even 30 hours. So could the Trial Chamber please take that into account. One of the major problems would be time restrictions in these proceedings that are otherwise evolving very nicely. So I always have to indicate when I did not examine a witness properly, and that can cast a shadow on the proceedings in total. But I am doing my best to deal with things as best I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider it. We'll be sitting in the morning, tomorrow morning; is it correct? Yes, 9.00. But before that, in a very general term, Mr. Tieger, whether you have any submission to make in relation to the witness who was supposed to appear after this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not aware that we've been apprised of additional information since we were last informed, and at that point -- well, I'm concerned about providing anything too fulsome and strained beyond the bounds of this point. May I suggest that we -- I don't have anything at this time, and may I suggest that we provide the Court with an answer, either in open or private session, at the first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now rising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.02 p.m.,
